title: Bayes' rule
summary: Turn P(positive | sick) into P(sick | positive): the law of total probability for P(positive), then Bayes' rule, on the 1% condition.

blocks.title: Sick and positive, as a probability

define.meaning: The share where $A$ happened, times the share of those where $B$ also did. It equals $P(A \text{ and } B)$.

blocks.why: Lesson 1 counted people. Bayes' rule does the same sums with probabilities, so you can use it when you have no table.
blocks.prompt: 1% of people are sick, and 90% of the sick test positive. What is $P(\text{sick and positive})$? Use $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)$.
hints: Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

blocks.title: Healthy and positive
blocks.why: The positives come from two groups. You need both.
blocks.prompt: 99% of people are healthy, and 5% of healthy people test positive. What is $P(\text{healthy and positive})$?

slips.say: That uses $\frac{1}{100}$, the sick share. The healthy share is $\frac{99}{100}$.

hints: Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

blocks.title: All positives

define.meaning: $P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \text{not } A)P(\text{not } A)$: split by the cases, add.

blocks.why: The bottom of Bayes' rule is the chance of testing positive at all. Sick and healthy people are the only two groups, so the two parts add.
blocks.prompt: $P(\text{sick and positive}) = \frac{9}{1000}$ and $P(\text{healthy and positive}) = \frac{99}{2000}$. Find $P(\text{positive})$.

slips.say: That adds $\frac{9}{1000}$ and $\frac{1}{20}$. The second part must be $\frac{1}{20} \times \frac{99}{100}$.

check.say: It should be $\frac{585}{10000}$ from lesson 1, the same number simplified.

blocks.title: Bayes' rule
blocks.why: Now divide: the share of positives that are sick.
blocks.prompt: $P(\text{sick}) = \frac{1}{100}$, $P(\text{positive} \mid \text{sick}) = \frac{9}{10}$, and $P(\text{positive}) = \frac{117}{2000}$. Use **Bayes' rule** $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$ to find $P(\text{sick} \mid \text{positive})$.

slips.say: That is $P(\text{positive} \mid \text{sick})$, the other direction. Bayes' rule flips it using the prior and $P(\text{positive})$.
That is the top only. Divide by $P(\text{positive})$.
That is $P(\text{positive})$. It belongs on the bottom.

hints: The top is $P(\text{sick and positive})$, which you found.
blocks.solution: Same $\frac{2}{13}$ as the table, now from probabilities alone. The prior $P(\text{sick})$ is what most people forget.

blocks.title: A much better test
blocks.why: Even a very good test can be weaker than it looks when the condition is rare.
blocks.prompt: 1% of people are sick. A new test is positive for 99% of the sick and for 1% of the healthy. Find $P(\text{sick} \mid \text{positive})$. Give a fraction.

slips.say: That is the sensitivity. Bayes' rule divides by all positives, which include the same number of healthy ones.
That is the prior. The test is positive, so the answer has moved a long way up.

hints: Top: $\frac{99}{100} \times \frac{1}{100}$. Bottom: that plus the healthy positives.

check.say: Count: of 10,000 people, 99 sick positives and 99 healthy positives.

blocks.solution: A 99% test on a 1% condition: a positive is a coin toss. The sick are rare, so their share is small even after a positive.
